claims.text: Equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength in its simple solid-solution state.
The relatively low hardness and strength of this CoCrFeNiTi alloy are caused by a minimal degree of short-range order in its FCC lattice.
Insufficient SRO lowers the energy barriers encountered by moving dislocations because fewer SRO-related stacking-fault and diffuse-antiphase-boundary penalties are generated.
Lower barriers to dislocation motion enable easier plastic deformation.
The proposed low-SRO state maintains good ductility and machinability.
The starting material is an equimolar or nearly equimolar, single-phase FCC CoCrFeNiTi solid solution.
Rapid solidification or quenching suppresses SRO development in CoCrFeNiTi.
Extended annealing at approximately 600 °C will promote SRO in CoCrFeNiTi.
SRO can be quantified using diffuse scattering, high-resolution microscopy, or local chemical-ordering analysis.
SRO is associated with higher stacking-fault energy and a large resistance to leading-partial motion.
Dislocation slip through an SRO-containing FCC lattice creates diffuse antiphase boundaries by disrupting local chemical order.
The energy penalties from stacking-fault creation and diffuse-antiphase-boundary generation exert back stress and retard dislocation motion.
Retarded dislocation motion enhances solid-solution strengthening.
Increasing SRO will increase both hardness and compressive or tensile strength.
Increasing SRO may slightly reduce ductility.
The mechanism is expected to apply to FCC CoCrFeNiTi at low strain rates and temperatures no higher than a vaguely defined moderate-temperature regime.
Dislocation-mediated plasticity is dominant within the proposed temperature and strain-rate limits.
The magnitude of the hardness and strength increase depends on annealing parameters and diffusion kinetics.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant hardness and strength increase after confirmed SRO development would falsify SRO as the primary strengthening mediator.
